stem:
The following frequency distribution shows the daily wages (in Rs) of 40 workers:

Wages (Rs): 100-120, 120-140, 140-160, 160-180, 180-200
Frequency:   4,       8,       14,       10,       4

What is the median wage?

per_option_rationale.rationale: 155 arises from using (20-12)/14 * 20 = 160/14 = 11.43 but rounding to 15 before adding to 140, giving 155.
148.57 comes from using cumulative frequency 26 as the numerator component instead of 20 (the n/2 target), i.e., (20 - 6)/14 * 20 + 140.
160 is taken as the upper boundary of the median class; the student stops at identifying the class but does not interpolate.

explanation: n = 40, so n/2 = 20. Cumulative frequencies: 4, 12, 26, 36, 40. The median class is 140-160 (cumulative frequency first exceeds 20 at 26). Using the interpolation formula: Median = L + ((n/2 - cf) / f) * h = 140 + ((20 - 12) / 14) * 20 = 140 + (8/14) * 20 = 140 + 11.43 = Rs 151.43.

explanation_sections.punchline: The interpolation formula locates the exact point within the median class where cumulative frequency crosses n/2.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: grouped data with equal class width. Build cumulative frequencies, locate the class where cf first >= n/2 = 20. Apply: Median = L + ((n/2 - cf_prev)/f_median)*h, where L=140, cf_prev=12, f=14, h=20.
explanation_sections.lesson: Use the cumulative frequency just before the median class (not the class boundary cf) in the numerator of the interpolation fraction.
explanation_sections.timing: 75 s. Build cf column (4, 12, 26, 36, 40), locate median class, plug into formula. The trap is using the wrong cf_prev.
